Dimanche matin, je suis allée courir. Mo: On Sunday morning, I went for a run. My new route takes me along du Parc Avenue, near Milton Street, and sometimes I stop to chat with people in the area. Last Sunday, after saying hello, a few people told me that their friend had been killed. They wanted to talk about it, and I listened.
Je dirais que, pour cet article, certain: I would say that, for this article, some of the challenges we faced were logistical. It’s important to be on the ground to report in person, but the current COVID-19 situation sometimes makes that difficult. It is also hard to talk to people who are grieving and already going through so much. This story pushed me to go further, to look at the tensions inherent in any human experience.
La première fois que j'ai rencontré Glor:
The first time I met Gloria André, she asked me: “Why are you trying to get information about my cousin?” That question stayed with me throughout the preparation of this report. Why do stories like Raphaël André’s matter? Why is it important to tell them? Because these lives matter. These stories matter.


Hi, it’s Kijâtai!
Lundi a débuté à La Converse mon stage e: On Monday, I started my journalism internship at La Converse. I’m thrilled to have this incredible opportunity to learn more about the profession and, at the same time, to develop journalistic skills that will allow me to help people representing the whole of Montréal’s urban community make their voices heard.
Mon premier jour de stage a aussi été un: My first day as an intern was also a deeply sad one, since it was the day we learned of the death of Raphaël Napa André. When I was asked to work with Cara on an article about this event, I have to admit that I hesitated at first. I wondered whether I was ready to tackle such a sensitive subject. I remember the effect Joyce’s video had on all of us and how difficult that period was. Did I have the energy to get through another tragedy? The difference, however, was that this time I had a way to channel all those feelings of sadness, anger and outrage by helping to write this article. I was able to speak with people who expressed their concerns and their feelings, but also their hope that things will change.
Et le changement commence avec la sensib: And change starts with awareness and dialogue. I hope that with this article we succeed in offering another perspective on Montréal’s urban Indigenous community and in starting a real discussion that will lead us toward solutions.
Dans le refuge Open Door, un mur commémo: At the Open Door shelter, a memorial wall honours the memory of members of the homeless community who used the shelter and have died. “They have all died since the start of the pandemic,” says coordinator John Tessier, pointing to the last six photos, those of Diana Matte, Kitty Kakernerk, Philip Magwa Haymond, Billy, Maurice Mooshoom and Mustafa Muhammed. “Now there will be seven, since we’ll have to add Raphaël’s,” he says.
Raphaël Napa André a été retrouvé sans v: Raphaël Napa André was found dead on Sunday morning at the corner of Milton Street and du Parc Avenue, less than a block from the shelter’s door. He is the third Indigenous homeless person to die at the corner of these streets since the start of the pandemic, a spot where many homeless Indigenous people gather.
Dimanche matin, à notre arrivée, le corp: On Sunday morning, when we arrived, Raphaël André’s frozen body lay covered with a yellow tarp next to a portable toilet. Milton Street was closed off with orange tape between du Parc Avenue and Jeanne-Mance Street.
« La porte était verrouillée », raconte: “The door was locked,” says Lizzie Akpahatak, describing how she found her friend a few hours earlier. “I came back, maybe an hour later, and the door was open... I saw him, and I told them, ‘I think there’s a dead man in the portable toilet.’”
Lizzie est assise, en compagnie de quelq: Lizzie is sitting with a few other people on the steps of an empty shop on du Parc Avenue. She points to the flashing lights of the police cars and media vehicles. “The police finally came this morning; they’re still there,” she says.
En 24 heures, la nouvelle de la mort de: Within 24 hours, the news of Raphaël’s death sparked strong concerns about homeless people, COVID-19 health restrictions in shelters and the provincial curfew that had just been introduced. Debates multiplied. Anger is rising. Nearly a week after the tragedy, as people are still trying to understand what happened to Raphaël André, other homeless people are wondering whether they will be next.
« J’espère que la vérité finira par sort: “I hope the truth will eventually come out,” says his friend Dany Charlish, who is also Innu. “Someone was there, there were people there. People believe Open Door closed at 9:30 and Napa went straight to the toilet at 9:35 to sit there? No, no, he didn’t go there at 9:35 to sit there. He was in the area... He was with people... and then he was found all alone. Where are those people?” he asks. “There are a lot of crack dealers around Milton and du Parc. That’s the sad truth nobody talks about. My friends, my Inuit friends, my Indigenous friends are under a lot of pressure,” he says. “They’re being preyed upon by these dealers. They go after us.”
Malgré les divers rapports établis, la c: Despite the various reports, the cause of Raphaël’s death remains unknown. Some think he sat down in the toilet where he was found because he was looking for shelter from the cold. Others think he was hiding from the police or had been attacked by drug dealers over money. Raphaël’s friends nevertheless believe that the circumstances of his death are suspicious. For its part, the Service de police de la Ville de Montréal (SPVM) has opened an investigation while awaiting the results of the coroner’s report.
« Pourquoi fermer Open Door à 9 h 30 ? »: “Why close Open Door at 9:30?” asks Nakuset, whose Native Women’s Shelter of Montréal stays open after curfew. Réal McKenzie, chief of the Innu community of Matimekush-Lac John, where the deceased came from, is asking the same question. Many people believe that exempting homeless people from curfew restrictions and opening more shelters would have prevented Raphaël André’s tragic death. Following this tragedy and the outcry it provoked, François Legault announced the opening of two more shelters last Thursday. In the meantime, we tried to understand what led to Open Door’s early closure.
Le 17 décembre, ce refuge a dû cesser se: On December 17, the shelter had to suspend its operations after four cases of COVID-19 were confirmed there and a plumbing problem was identified. Homeless people were temporarily moved to the Chrome hotel while work was carried out at the shelter. The premises were also disinfected, and new safety measures were put in place.
Selon le CIUSSS du Centre-Ouest-de-l’Île: According to the CIUSSS du Centre-Ouest-de-l’Île-de-Montréal, Open Door was authorized to reopen on January 11, but only as a daytime shelter. The CIUSSS said it had issued 13 recommendations to allow the shelter to reopen 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, and is still waiting for these measures to be put in place.
« Ce n’est pas vrai », s’insurge John Te: “That’s not true,” says an outraged John Tessier, who maintains that Open Door never received a list of recommendations, despite the shelter’s many attempts to contact the CIUSSS. He also insists that it is hard to understand why, if such safety measures were so necessary, the CIUSSS would have allowed the shelter to resume operations. “If there are 13 recommendations meant to ensure our safety, and they haven’t been implemented, well... why are we open right now?” he asks, exasperated.
Open Door affirme que son seul objectif,: Open Door says its only goal right now is to have a shelter accessible 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, as soon as possible. “People need a place to sleep and rest, a place where they’re safe and aren’t forced to prostitute themselves or get raped at the crack-filled hotel down the street,” says Mr. Tessier. “It would be nice to be able to help people all year round.”
Isabelle Sawyer a été l’une des dernière: Isabelle Sawyer was one of the last people to see Raphaël alive. She gave him a sleeping bag when he left the shelter on the night of Saturday to Sunday. Later, she wrote a message that was published on the website of the <l1>Comité Citoyen de Milton Parc (CCMP)</l1>. “As a society, we let the most vulnerable down by wasting so much time blaming one another and ‘doing our part’; even though each of the system’s funded services is trying to be efficient and beyond reproach, people aren’t getting the services they need,” she writes.
Les problèmes découlant des restrictions: The problems stemming from COVID-19 restrictions don’t end there. There is also the murky question of who is responsible for enforcing them. In a statement to the <l1>Journal de Montréal,</l1> the Direction régionale de santé publique (DRSP) said it did not have the authority to close the Open Door shelter. As a result, even if the centre were to remain open, it is unclear whether that would break the law or whether it would constitute grounds for closing it. It is not even clear where such directives would come from.
La Converse a communiqué avec le service: La Converse contacted the SPVM’s media relations department to ask whether the police intended to enforce the recommendations issued to establishments by public health authorities. The SPVM offered no comment on the matter. The Service says the task does not fall under its jurisdiction, although it does have the authority to enforce mask-wearing, physical distancing and the provincial curfew.

À en juger par l’effet qu’a eu sa mort,: Judging by the impact of his death, Raphaël had close ties to Montréal’s urban Indigenous community, of which he was a part. According to his friends, he frequented the Native Friendship Centre of Montréal and Projets Autochtones du Québec (PAQ), where he is described as a friendly man, a good person and someone very funny. Many members of the community were shocked to learn of the tragic circumstances of his death.
« Je l’ai reçu chez moi à Noël, raconte: “I had him over at my place at Christmas,” says Gloria André, Raphaël’s cousin and one of the only members of his family living in Montréal. “He seemed a bit down, like he didn’t know where to go.”
Chez PAQ, Gloria écoute de la musique av: At PAQ, Gloria is listening to music with a group of friends. “Why do you want to know his story?” she asks from behind a surgical mask. A deep sadness fills her dark eyes. “It brings up a lot of emotions,” she says, unable to say more.
À ses côtés se trouve Dany Charlish, un: Beside her is Dany Charlish, a friend of Raphaël’s from Mashteuiatsh, in Lac-Saint-Jean. He says Raphaël had travelled back and forth between Montréal and Quebec City several times over the past few years, but that in September he was doing well and had a place to live. “Napa was doing well last summer,” he says. “He was doing well. He wasn’t smoking cannabis, he wasn’t drinking... I don’t know what happened since September. He had a place, and now he had nowhere to go.”
Dany dit avoir vu son ami mercredi derni: Dany says he saw his friend last Wednesday. They took a photo, which now carries the caption RIP on Facebook. “He wanted to go have a cigarette,” he remembers. “I said no because I had COVID-19. I feel bad about that now... That’s the last time I saw him.”
Jennifer Brazeau, présidente du CA de Mo: Jennifer Brazeau, chair of the board of Montréal Autochtone and executive director of the Centre d’amitié autochtone de Lanaudière, has worked extensively for urban Indigenous communities throughout her career. Raphaël André was known to those around her, she notes, adding that the Indigenous community in Montréal is large but tightly knit. “It hits us one way or another, even if there might be 10,000 of us in Montréal. We’re all connected in one way or another. It’s like one big family in Montréal. We’ve lost our brothers.”
Dans la ville natale de Raphaël, Matimek: In Raphaël’s hometown, Matimekush-Lac John, Chief Réal McKenzie is waiting for the deceased’s body to be repatriated. “Everyone is in mourning in the big Innu family of Matimekush-Lac John,” he tells us over the phone. He remains perplexed by the tragic death of Raphaël, who kept in daily contact with his mother. “Could we have saved him somehow? I don’t know... In a way, yes... There are still people in Montréal,” he says, adding that he can’t understand the circumstances of his death.
Si la mort de Raphaël André a suscité un: While Raphaël André’s death has provoked a public outcry, community members don’t want his story to get lost in the news cycle. Dany Charlish says he doesn’t know what happened or how Raphaël ended up on the street, but that it is a common experience for Indigenous people in urban settings.
Melissa Mollen Dupuis, activiste de la N: Melissa Mollen Dupuis, an Innu activist who has often raised awareness of Indigenous realities, was one of the many people who voiced their concerns on social media after articles reporting Raphaël’s death were published.
« C’est vrai qu’il y a une situation lié: “It’s true that there’s something tied to our culture, a communal solidarity, so that when I’m in Mingan, I know I’ll never go hungry, I know I’ll have a place to sleep,” she says. “The problem is that my community doesn’t have the resources to do that indefinitely,” she adds, explaining the displacement of Indigenous people to urban areas.
« Parfois aussi, la communauté que tu va: “Sometimes, too, the community you find in the city is already on the street. It’s part of a struggle. You feel like it’s your place. But it’s also that we feel we have our place on our reserves and that, when we come to the city, we’re displaced,” she notes.
La mort de Raphaël André est-elle un sym: Is Raphaël André’s death a symptom of a sick system? she is asked. The co-founder of Idle No More Quebec answers by offering some avenues for reflection.
« Est-ce que Raphaël a vu le policier co: “Did Raphaël see the police officer as someone who could help him or as someone who would ostracize him?” she asks. “Why couldn’t he see him as someone who could help? Why is it that Joyce, our mothers, our grandmothers, our aunts, our uncles go to hospitals and see someone they’re not sure will help them?”
<strong>Des solutions pour tenter de rés: Solutions to try to resolve the crisis
Pas moins de 192 personnes itinérantes o: No fewer than 192 homeless people have tested positive for COVID-19 in Montréal since December, according to the Direction de la santé publique de Montréal. As frontline workers become increasingly scarce and shelters struggle to stay open, many people experiencing homelessness say they have feared for their lives since the start of the pandemic. Faced with this situation, Jennifer Brazeau believes governments should take frontline workers’ recommendations into consideration. “Rather than closing shelters and warming centres, we should be investing to make these places safe spaces. That would be one of the first ways to save the lives of members of a community that is quite vulnerable to this disease,” she suggests.
La famille de Raphaël « Napa » André pré: The family of Raphaël “Napa” André is preparing his funeral in Matimekush. It will take place on January 29. Chief Réal McKenzie will say a prayer on the community radio station with “a very deep thought for him, his family and the community in general.” At the site of his death, a frozen white rose lies in memory of the 51-year-old man. Starting January 25, people will be able to pay their respects at the intersection of Milton Street and du Parc Avenue.
